question.questionText: By Christmas, I _____ for Mr. Smith for six years.
question.explanationHtml:
Detailed Explanation:
The blank requires the correct tense to indicate an action that will have been happening for a period of time up to a specific point in the future (by Christmas). The correct tense for this situation is the future perfect continuous (will have been + V-ing), which is used to show the duration of an action up to a certain future moment.
  • will have been working (verb phrase): Future perfect continuous tense: used to describe an action that will continue up until a point in the future.
  • will work (verb phrase): Simple future tense: describes an action that will happen in the future, but does not emphasize duration.
  • have been working (verb phrase): Present perfect continuous tense: describes an action that started in the past and continues to the present, not to a future point.
  • will be working (verb phrase): Future continuous tense: describes an action that will be happening at a specific time in the future, but does not emphasize duration up to that point.
Related structure or vocabulary: Future perfect continuous tense: S + will have been + V-ing + (for/since + time). Used to show how long something will have been happening by a certain future time.

question.questionText: She ______ the living room when she heard a strange noise in the kitchen.
question.explanationHtml:
Detailed Explanation:
In this sentence, we need to choose the correct verb tense to describe an action that was happening in the past when another action interrupted it. The structure for this situation is: Past Continuous (was/were + V-ing) for the ongoing action, and Simple Past for the action that interrupts. Here, 'she ______ the living room' is the ongoing action, and 'she heard a strange noise' is the interrupting action.
  • has cleaned (verb (Present Perfect)): Present Perfect tense, used to describe an action that happened at an unspecified time before now. Not suitable here because the sentence describes two actions in the past.
  • has been (verb (Present Perfect)): Incomplete verb phrase; 'has been' needs a complement (e.g., 'has been cleaning'). Alone, it is incorrect.
  • cleaning (verb (V-ing)): V-ing form, but without an auxiliary verb, it cannot stand alone as the main verb in this sentence.
  • was cleaning (verb (Past Continuous)): Past Continuous tense, used to describe an action that was ongoing in the past when another action occurred. This fits the context perfectly.
Related structure or vocabulary: Past Continuous tense: was/were + V-ing is used to describe an action that was in progress at a specific time in the past, often interrupted by another action in the Simple Past.

question.questionText: You arrived two days ago. You are going to leave next Sunday. By the time you leave, you ........... nine days here.

Detailed Explanation:
The blank requires the correct verb tense to indicate an action that will be completed before a specific time in the future. The phrase 'By the time you leave' refers to a future point, and the action (spending nine days) will be finished by then. The correct tense for this situation is the future perfect tense: 'will have spent.'
  • spend (verb (base form)): Base form of the verb, used for present simple or infinitive, not suitable for this future perfect context.
  • have spent (verb (present perfect)): Present perfect tense, used for actions completed at an unspecified time before now, not for actions completed before a future time.
  • are spending (verb (present continuous)): Present continuous tense, used for actions happening now or around now, not for actions completed before a future time.
  • will have spent (verb (future perfect)): Future perfect tense, used for actions that will be completed before a specific time in the future. This is the correct answer.
Related structure or vocabulary: Future perfect tense: will have + past participle. Used to describe an action that will be completed before a specific time in the future. Example: By next year, I will have graduated.

question.questionText: Where is he? I _____ for him since three o'clock!
question.explanationHtml:
Detailed Explanation:
The blank requires a verb tense that shows an action started in the past and is still continuing up to the present. The phrase 'since three o'clock' indicates the action began at a specific time in the past and is ongoing. The Present Perfect Continuous tense (have/has been + V-ing) is used to express this idea.
  • am waiting (verb phrase): Present Continuous tense, used for actions happening right now, not for actions that started in the past and continue to the present.
  • have been waiting (verb phrase): Present Perfect Continuous tense, used for actions that started in the past and are still continuing now, especially with 'since' or 'for'.
  • was waiting (verb phrase): Past Continuous tense, used for actions that were happening at a specific time in the past, not continuing to the present.
  • had been waiting (verb phrase): Past Perfect Continuous tense, used for actions that were ongoing in the past before another past action.
Related structure or vocabulary: Present Perfect Continuous tense: have/has been + V-ing. Used to describe actions that started in the past and continue to the present, often with 'since' (for a point in time) or 'for' (for a duration).

question.questionText: He said that his mother would be very upset when she _______ that he had lost his job.
question.explanationHtml:
Detailed Explanation:

The action “learned” occurs at the same time as the reaction “would be very upset,” not before it in a way that requires emphasizing the sequence of events. Therefore, the simple past tense is the most appropriate choice.

  • A. learns: present tense, which is not suitable after the reporting verb “said.”

  • B. learned: simple past tense, correct for the when-clause and appropriate in meaning.

  • C. had learned: past perfect, which is unnecessary because there is no need to emphasize a before–after relationship.

  • D. would learn: would is not used in time clauses beginning with when.

Related structure or vocabulary: 

When / after / before → prefer the simple past; use had + past participle only when it is necessary to clearly emphasize sequence.

  • B. learned: thì quá khứ đơn, đúng với mệnh đề when và đúng ngữ nghĩa.

  • C. had learned: quá khứ hoàn thành, không cần thiết vì không có sự nhấn mạnh trước–sau.

  • D. would learn: không dùng would trong mệnh đề thời gian bắt đầu bằng when.
